622382375.en:
@_**Jacob Lifshay|229517** [said](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/122651-general/topic/False.20positive.20.60deny.28static_mut_refs.29.60/near/622382170):
```quote
note the `A[i]` operation is a compiler built-in (only when `i: usize`) -- it doesn't actually call any library code, unlike the `get_unchecked` function call
```

Does that matter for reference liveness? I would assume it behaves exactly like a library call for e.g. stacked borrows.

@_* * Jacob Lifshay | 229517 * * [说] （https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/122651-general/topic/False.20positive.20.60deny.28static_mut_refs.29.60/near/622382170):

note the `A[i]` operation is a compiler built-in (only when `i: usize`) -- it doesn't actually call any library code, unlike the `get_unchecked` function call

622408943.en: If there exists a mutable reference to an element of `A` while `a`/`b` is called for a *different* element, `a` does not conflict with that since it only accesses one element, but `b` does conflict since it takes a shared reference to `A` as a whole.  https://play.rust-lang.org/?version=stable&mode=debug&edition=2024&gist=d6e5e38ffdc54fe3c44009e19ec8b0e3 (This example fails under current stacked borrows and tree borrows)
622408943.zh: 如果存在对以下元素的可变引用：`A`在安装时发生错误 %1$s: %2$s.`a`/`b`被调用为*不同的*元素，`a`不会与之冲突，因为它只访问一个元素，但`b`发生冲突，因为它需要一个共享的引用`A`决议草案六全文https://play.rust-lang.org/?version=stable&mode=debug&edition=2024&gist=d6e5e38ffdc54fe3c44009e19ec8b0e3（此示例在当前堆叠借用和树借用下失败）

622500530.en: iirc the documentation is generally something like: "just use it through raw pointers, don't create references to mutable statics".
622500530.zh: 文档通常是这样的： “只需通过原始指针使用它，不要创建对可变静态的引用”。

622501133.en: so using `A[i]` technically works because it's a compiler built-in, but it's mostly in the same category as calling methods that implicitly make references and stuff so imo you shouldn't do it on mutable statics, use pointers instead.
622501133.zh: 所以使用`A[i]`技术上是可行的，因为它是一个内置的编译器，但它大多与调用隐式生成引用和内容的方法属于同一类别，因此IMO您不应该在可变静态上执行此操作，而应使用指针。

some programmers would pass a `long` or pointer directly, which is UB, though it kinda worked on most 32-bit systems and a few 64-bit systems.

如果这是关于`makecontext`仅允许您传递`int`到被调用的函数，可以很好地使用它来传递指针，您只需将指针转换为`usize`，然后将其拆分为`int`-大块头。

620226712.en:
We currently have the following list of `target_arch` values getting set for mips targets:

```text
 #                   tgt                             cfg
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  0   mips-mti-none-elf                      target_arch="mips"
  1   mips-unknown-linux-gnu                 target_arch="mips"
  2   mips-unknown-linux-musl                target_arch="mips"
  3   mips-unknown-linux-uclibc              target_arch="mips"
  4   mips64-openwrt-linux-musl              target_arch="mips64"
  5   mips64-unknown-linux-gnuabi64          target_arch="mips64"
  6   mips64-unknown-linux-muslabi64         target_arch="mips64"
  7   mips64el-unknown-linux-gnuabi64        target_arch="mips64"
  8   mips64el-unknown-linux-muslabi64       target_arch="mips64"
  9   mipsel-mti-none-elf                    target_arch="mips"
 10   mipsel-sony-psp                        target_arch="mips"
 11   mipsel-sony-psx                        target_arch="mips"
 12   mipsel-unknown-linux-gnu               target_arch="mips"
 13   mipsel-unknown-linux-musl              target_arch="mips"
 14   mipsel-unknown-linux-uclibc            target_arch="mips"
 15   mipsel-unknown-netbsd                  target_arch="mips"
 16   mipsel-unknown-none                    target_arch="mips"
 17   mipsisa32r6-unknown-linux-gnu          target_arch="mips32r6"
 18   mipsisa32r6el-unknown-linux-gnu        target_arch="mips32r6"
 19   mipsisa64r6-unknown-linux-gnuabi64     target_arch="mips64r6"
 20   mipsisa64r6el-unknown-linux-gnuabi64   target_arch="mips64r6"
```

Does it really make sense to set a `mips32r6` and `mips64r6` `target_arch`, rather than reusing `mips` and `mips64`? Reading through section 2.3.6 at https://s3-eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/downloads-mips/documents/MD00083-2B-MIPS64INT-AFP-06.01.pdf it seems like there are instruction differences that you need to be aware of writing asm, but otherwise don't matter.

It feels like this could be something encoded via `target_abi` now that we have it.

(Added in https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/58941, for context)

606382523.en:
While I have no objection to dropping i686 host tools, demoing to tier 2 is a worry.

To quote a colleague "x86 will outlive the sun" - building apps as i686 is still very important, especially if you want to support older versions of Windows. x64 emulation for Arm64 is only supported on Win11, so i686 is the only thing guaranteed to work on any version or arch of Windows.

606410928.en:
> the target not exactly having a future by the OS vendor

This is not entirely true; the host tools don't, but there are no (public) deprecation plans for WOW64. That being said, I don't think running host tools on 32-bit Windows editions is relevant anymore, and that we should drop the host tools.

i686-msvc is in a bit of a funny situation: It leeches its maintenance off of x86-64, which works fine for the library side, and the interest in that target is much more skewed towards the enterprise space - there is still a lot of software only providing 32-bit builds, and if you have to interoperate with that, you need the ability to compile 32-bit code. It also generally works, as opposed to, say, the GNU version.

Assuming the i686-msvc CI seizing up doesn't become a more regular occurrence, and with only this issue in mind, I'd be in favor of dropping it to T1 without host tools. I think a demotion to T2 (which, even if we run tests, signals a level of instability simply due to its neighborhood currently not present in the target) would only fit at this moment if we also want to clean out some of the legacy brokenness in 32-bit tier 1 targets, like the wonders of x87 or alignment issues (like MSVC aligning i64 to 4 bytes if it's on the stack).

606784620.en:
@_**Jonathan 'theJPster' Pallant|203633** [said](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/131828-t-compiler/topic/Demoting.20.60i686-pc-windows-msvc.60.20to.20Tier.202.3F/near/606402767):
```quote
But the host tools do not seem useful because I don’t know how much you can compile with just 2GB of virtual address space per process.
```

TBH, I think we should never have any 32-bit *hosts* as "with host tools" at tier 1.  There's a bunch of stuff that definitely has bugs if you cross-compile from 32-bit host to 64-bit target, for example.  And I think we should just "won't fix" any bugs related to having <3GB of address space while running rustc.

We can still consider "excessive memory usage" bugs, but I think we should just pre-emptively decide not to care about 32-bit address space for *host tools*.

@_**Fulgen|644580** [said](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/131828-t-compiler/topic/Demoting.20.60i686-pc-windows-msvc.60.20to.20Tier.202.3F/near/606406385):
```quote
You can get more than 2GB when the binary is large address aware, but for a compiler, it's...not much change. 
```

Yeah, I consider the difference between 2GB and 3GB here completely irrelevant.

609293220.en:
Normally (in Visual Studio or windbg) it autoswitches to the 32-bit debugger. If you explicitely force the 64-bit debugger it can properly debug it, but you're debugging it from a 64-bit point of view, which exposes you to all the WOW64 stuff like how it does CPU mode switching from 32bit to 64bit for syscalls etc. Not useful, and generally not done.

And also not really what we care about if we want to test debuginfo.

611999759.en:
> Unfortunately, while `i686-unknown-linux-gnu` performs better in some regards, it also currently fails some of the upcoming criteria even more severely.
It is thus unclear whether `i686-unknown-linux-gnu` should remain a tier 1 or tier 2 target. However, it *does* maintain upstream support.
It is still possible to compile a recent Linux kernel that runs on a 32-bit x86 CPU, and many software distributions offer it significant support.
Thus, it is not part of this RFC, because there is nothing to be consistent about when the factors for a different target are inconsistent with another.

564775102.en:
Not to hijack the discussion too much, but one thing I miss from gdb + C++ in gdb + rust is that of python replacements for functions: basically something like the indexing operator for a std::vector would also have a python implementation in the debugger.

Rust just have the pretty printers, but if you have a *large* collection (let's say hundreds or more items) gdb will unhelpfully print `...` and not show them all. Plus if you have that many items it is hard to see what is going on visually anyway.

Having an indexing operator that you can *call* from gdb is a game changer to be able to print sub fields of items, or check if an item is in a set, etc.

But for some unfathomable reason it seems the focus so far has only been on the pretty printers.

I might be the odd one out but for debugging I actually strongly prefer command line debuggers. I really don't want to debug from an IDE, and for IDEs I prefer something more light weight like vscode. (And yes, it feels strange to call vscode light weight.)

The IDE debuggers never expose the full power, or at least make it quite awkward to interact directly with the underlying debugger to do something like set a hardware memory watchpoint. And woe betide you if you want to write some custom adhoc python or send a custom monitor command to your gdb server (eg. for talking directly to valgrind, or to your hardware debugger hooked up to your microcontroller over JTAG).

Working directly with the command line debugger just has less "impedance mismatch" and it doesn't get in your way.

566715120.en:
>I don't know if lldb supports that.

In terms of indexing, sortof. The visualizer scripts allow one to index using the variable display command (e.g. `v vec[1]`), but iirc it doesn't work in the expression parser (e.g. `expr vec[1]`) for (slightly stupid) reasons.

The short of it is that visualization is handled ~language-agnostically, whereas expression parsing needs a bespoke plugin for your language. LLDB's expression-parser plugin architecture is like... *really*  hands-off, for better and worse.  It literally hands you a string and the current stack frame and then waits for you to return an object that represents the result of the expression. That means you need to write literally an entire interpreter for it to work as expected. There's an example of that [here](https://github.com/tromey/lldb/tree/a0fc10ce0dacb3038b7302fff9f6cb8cb34b37c6/source/Plugins/ExpressionParser/Rust). One nice thing is it would allow us to just plug in something like MIRI, rustc itself, or [excvr](https://github.com/evcxr/evcxr) pretty easily though.

>The main issue with lldb is that it isn't ergonomic. You can see that in that gdb has all sorts of short names for common operations, like `b` to set a breakpoint, or `c` to continue. While lldb doesn't.

IIRC LLDB's commands can all be abbreviated. If the abbreviation is unambiguous, it will work. It also has a number of hard-coded abbreviations, including `b` for `breakpoint set`, `c` for `continue`, and `v` for `frame variable`, `n` for step over, `s` for step into, etc.

It also has `command alias` that allow users to specify their own command abbreviations.

566716809.en:
>it would be awesome if the debugger knew how to call a `Debug` impl of a value if it can't otherwise render it nicely

Within an expression support plugin in LLDB, you can tell it how to call Rust functions, so this should be possible. I don't know if GDB has an equivalent, but i'd assume it does. One issue though is that if the debug impl is never used, iirc doesn't end up in the binary even if compiled in debug mode.

For debug impls that are in the binary though, i think you might even be able to do this right now with lldb's existing commands called from the python visualizer scripts?  `register write rcx <ptr to struct>` -> `jump <debug impl addr>` -> `thread step-out` -> `register read rax`

Saving/restoring the correct registers for the calling convention should be pretty simple, though I'm not sure exactly how you'd handle the `&mut Formatter` that needs to be passed in. I'd need to look into it more

````quote
`yeet1` or `yeet2` -- since `trap` is clearly different, it has a different type signature
````
sorry i am new to this conversation, but the way i see it, `yeet1` and `yeet2` should probably have different type signatures. 
after all few things make behavior more clear than good typing.

`yeet1` should return a `FakeInhabited` type, with a safe `ex_nihilo::<T>(self) -> T` method that calls  `unreacheable_unchecked`, but would not otherwise register as uninhabited to the compiler, meaning producing it would not immediately mark the following code as unreacheable.
that would properly enshrine the fact that the following code is unreacheable (it is not possible to have `FakeInhabited` in safe reacheable code) but the compiler isn't aware of it unless we tell it.

`FakeInhabited` is actually a quite convenient type to have when one whishes to check ghost branches of code without having the borrow checker go "oh, an uninhabited type was produced, let's just ignore everything that follows"

I think it would be very weird for us to have something called `breakpoint` which doesn't match what other languages do. And I think even if we want a breakpoint with special ub semantics, we'd still want the underlying thing that others use (aka yeet2 in the summary).

I don't love the longer name (`breakpoint_assume_noop`) for it but I'd live with it if it means we can stabilise something.

622616082.en:
It is in `core::arch` so I would kind of expect it to just follow platform semantics (although I guess it should really be in `core::os` since it's OS dependent). My problem with the longer names is they should ideally encapsulate that what it does can vary by platform, even if, the most common behaviour is consistent. We could also guard it with `is_debugger_attached()` but I don't think that's a good idea for the more primitive thing (and some platforms may not have a way to test for debugger presence).

But again, I'd be happy with any proposal that can gain consensus even if I think it less than ideal. We can stabilise whatever we call `yeet2` today but `yeet1` hasn't been implemented yet so we don't have to finalise its name (although having some idea would be good).

yeet2: whenever you write `breakpoint()` you have to make sure that it's okay for that to be a NOP, and the code that runs after `breakpoint()` returns (if it returns) has to run without UB.
or, equivalently: if your code becomes unsound when I replace `breakpoint()` by a NOP, then your code was already unsound before I did that.

Are these the rules we'd want for yeet2 semantics?

1. The only guarantee is that `breakpoint` will act as either a nop or an abort
2. If a debugger is attached, it should pause on `breakpoint()` but allow resuming (net nop)
3. If a debugger is not attached or if we have no way to do (2), `breakpoint()` *should* abort, but it is also defined behavior to be a nop
4. In Miri and CTFE (if we add that), `breakpoint` is a nop

622708276.en:
@_**RalfJ|120791** [said](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/219381-t-libs/topic/Pushing.20.60breakpoint.60.20over.20the.20finish.20line.3F/near/622662594):
```quote
yeet2: whenever you write `breakpoint()` you have to make sure that it's okay for that to be a NOP, and the code that runs after `breakpoint()` returns (if it returns) has to run without UB.
or, equivalently: if your code becomes unsound when I replace `breakpoint()` by a NOP, then your code was already unsound before I did that.
```

I'm wondering if the recent discussions about "time-traveling UB" might be able to help here. Writing something like `breakpoint(); possible_ub();`, in the course of debugging `possible_ub()` is a lot like writing `eprintln!("about to maybe crash"); possible_ub();`, but stronger. In both cases, the UB of `possible_ub()` can't time-travel to before the previous statement, it can only happen after the breakpoint/eprintln. If you continue after the breakpoint, the program executes UB, and whatever that UB causes to happen will happen. If you *don't* continue after the breakpoint, the program didn't execute UB. (Just as, for instance, if you write "if the pointer is not null, dereference it", you aren't dereferencing a null pointer.)

598294774.en: To put it in folks’ brains: one thing I’m planning on doing soon is writing a series of blog posts building up the concepts of UB and soundness explained from ~first principles (the ~ is that I’m going to hand-wave *why* we have UB and just say “it’s bad don’t do it trust me”). The goal is to get to the point where I can exhaustively enumerate a complete and maximally-fine grained taxonomy of concepts related to language/library UB/soundness/invariant/etc. The hope is that any subsequent discussions about terminology can be expressed as “what sets of these maximally-fine grained terms should we lump together in our final set of official terminology?”

617267912.en:
Quoting from the proposal:

---

## Work this proposal is intended to coordinate

This package is intended to address, amend, or provide a common foundation for:
- [RFC 3845, `repr(ordered_fields)`](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/pull/3845),
  which separates declaration-ordered Rust layout from a future C layout;
- [RFC 3718, target/system C layouts](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/pull/3718),
  together with [RFC 3806, field-level alignment](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/pull/3806);
- the [zero-sized ABI compatibility work](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/157973),
  the related [`repr(transparent)` array work](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/155984),
  and [UCG issue #552](https://github.com/rust-lang/unsafe-code-guidelines/issues/552);
- [crABI](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/pull/3470), which translates
  higher-level types through a C-based ABI;
- proposals for [C bit-fields](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/pull/3113),
  [complex numbers](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/blob/master/text/3892-complex-numbers.md),
  and [scalable vectors](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/pull/3838); and
- open compiler and language questions around
  [call-ABI representation](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/119183),
  [profile-sensitive `VaList`](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/141618),
  and [nominal C types for cross-language CFI](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/pull/3296).

The claim is not that all of this work must land together. The claim is that it
should fit one coherent model before individual pieces establish incompatible
assumptions.

621521937.en:
Assuming that the `freeze(poison)` operation just non-deteministically produces a value, you’re basically asking if the non-determinism should somehow go away at the point of doing the IO, right? You say “If yes, that seems surprising” – I assume – because the *real* program of course is not going to be nondeterministic. The “real value” of demonic must be somehow in memory.. the real machine can’t be in a whole set of possible states all at once.

But I think the abstract machine model very well can just do that. Yes non-determinism is kinda weird, but that’s just the way the semantics are defined, and stripping away potential execution paths that emerged from non-determinism is a valid thing the compiler can do during compilation, and it’s a very natural thing [and it *will* happen during compilation just because somehow modeling multiple states at once sounds super expensive and unnecessary] but it’s not a thing that preserves ***equivalent*** semantics. Instead it’s a one-way route.

I hope I’m intuiting this stuff correctly, please correct me if I got this completely wrong.

(In case it wasn’t clear, I agree that f2 is equivalent to f1..)

You say “If yes, that seems surprising” – I assume – because the *real* program of course is not going to be nondeterministic. The “real value” of demonic must be somehow in memory.. the real machine can’t be in a whole set of possible states all at once.

But I think the abstract machine model very well can just do that. Yes non-determinism is kinda weird, but that’s just the way the semantics are defined, and stripping away potential execution paths that emerged from non-determinism is a valid thing the compiler can do during compilation, and it’s a very natural thing [and it *will* happen during compilation just because somehow modeling multiple states at once sounds super expensive and unnecessary] but it’s not a thing that preserves ***equivalent*** semantics. Instead it’s a one-way route.

I hope I’m intuiting this stuff correctly, please correct me if I got this completely wrong.

(In case it wasn’t clear, I agree that f2 is equivalent to f1..)

621607315.en:
My intuition is that f1 and f3 are not equivalent, and f3 is equivalent to f2.

f3 "obviously" can legally be compiled to always executing UB. One way to reasonably implement the freeze(poison) operation is by reusing the register that previously held user input, and using that register to store the `demonic` variable. (Edit: Actually, it would need to have the register's value somehow modified in between, like it being incremented or something, so that the comparison gives the result of "unequal". Still doesn't seem so implausible to happen though.)

If read() produces a random value from an external source, then f1 should have well-defined behavior with probability at least 1/256. After all, we've frozen the poison value, so after the freeze, it better act like a normal integer.

621780374.en:
@_**Frank Steffahn|280891** [said](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/136281-t-opsem/topic/Can.20IO.20provide.20angelic.20choice/near/621521937):
```quote
You say “If yes, that seems surprising” – I assume – because the *real* program of course is not going to be nondeterministic. The “real value” of demonic must be somehow in memory.. the real machine can’t be in a whole set of possible states all at once.
```

Our semantics also isn't in a whole set of states at the same time. The AM can sometimes make a non-deterministic choice, but it *has to choose*. In `f1`, by the time you reach the read, the AM (at least as we specify it currently) has already committed to a value of `demonic`; however that value is not leaked through an observable event.

If you want to make `f1` and `f2` equivalent, you have to specify that input can only depend what is observable so far (which is complicated to make fully precise, but at least includes the trace of observable events to this point). Or you need some way to postpone the choice of the particular value for `demonic`, e.g. by modelling variables to have a set of values instead of a single value (but here I'm thinking of variables as SSA values/registers, not as stack allocated objects, because that would be much more complicated to define such non-det semantics for).

621866355.en:
Here's a (hopefully equivalent) alternative model that hurts my head less to reason about. My understanding is that the wording of the C standard implies this model.

The abstract machine is an interpreter that doesn't just maintain the current program state. It maintains the *set* of all possible current program states, executing them in lockstep.

Each time a nondeterministic operation (such as freeze) is executed on one of the elements of this set, this one element gets forked into multiple elements.

Each time the program produces output (or any observable behavior) the interpreter uses the behavior of one of the current program states in the set, and deletes all states in the set that do not produce this observable behavior.

This model is obviously self-consistent, doesn't require time travel, handles nondeterministic environment with no further complications, and is easier to reason about. It's even potentially implementable as an actual interpreter.

@_**niluxv|401145** [said](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/136281-t-opsem/topic/.E2.9C.94.20Can.20IO.20provide.20angelic.20choice/near/621780374):
````quote
@_**Frank Steffahn|280891** [said](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/136281-t-opsem/topic/Can.20IO.20provide.20angelic.20choice/near/621521937):
```quote
You say “If yes, that seems surprising” – I assume – because the *real* program of course is not going to be nondeterministic. The “real value” of demonic must be somehow in memory.. the real machine can’t be in a whole set of possible states all at once.
```

Our semantics also isn't in a whole set of states at the same time. The AM can sometimes make a non-deterministic choice, but it *has to choose*. In `f1`, by the time you reach the read, the AM (at least as we specify it currently) has already committed to a value of `demonic`; however that value is not leaked through an observable event.

If you want to make `f1` and `f2` equivalent, you have to specify that input can only depend what is observable so far (which is complicated to make fully precise, but at least includes the trace of observable events to this point). Or you need some way to postpone the choice of the particular value for `demonic`, e.g. by modelling variables to have a set of values instead of a single value (but here I'm thinking of variables as SSA values/registers, not as stack allocated objects, because that would be much more complicated to define such non-det semantics for).
````

“Our semantics also isn't in a whole set of states at the same time.” but why not? At some level of abstraction perhaps the "abstract machine" makes a non-deterministic choice immediately; but if you look closer, couldn't that be just a tool to define state transitions more compactly as relations (rather than functions), whereas the “actual” non-deterministic choices aren't *really* made already (at least up to the point where they become observable)?

622424346.en:
I wouldn't describe them as "executing in lockstep" though, because different paths can go through *vastly* different amounts of execution steps before the next point of IO is reached.

Implementing an actual interpreter may run into issues if some paths take long to execute. (You can't exactly solve the halting problem to answer the question of what to expect in the long run.) That, and the state size can get huge of course.

```quote
I think it's also important that we can remove unnused variables

Otherwise after inlining we just have this huge mess of unused stuff on the stack
```

I mean, just being honest, I know how to write systems code if the compiler can't clean up the stack as well. The code is slower, but you can focus on hand-optimizing other parts to make up for that. (This is especially true for heap allocations, where it's better to just try and not perform the allocation if you won't need it. In practice, the compiler rarely is able to fully remove them anyway, especially these days due to the alloc_shim_is_unstable stuff (although the compiler can still remove the allocation in some cases despite that, I'm not claiming otherwise)).

Conversely, I'm not sure I know how to write systems code if I can't compare pointers anymore. (I mean, realistically, I think people will just have to do it anyway). Among many other things, it's hard to enforce safety in many cases with such restrictions.

621519125.en:
Thinking about this some more, I don't think overlapping allocations are necessary to justify most allocation-elision optimisations, as long as you stop assuming that stack allocations *always* succeed. If you change that to assuming that only a limited amount of stack space is always available (because in practise there *is* actually a guard-page worth of space that's guaranteed to be unused), you can still completely elide small allocations, as long as you can prove that they would fit into the remaining amount of stack. So the only change necessary is that optimisations have to prove that the total size of the elided allocations is smaller than the remaining-stack-space constant (i.e. the size of the guard page). But as long as that space *could* have been available, there is no need to *actually* allocate anything in the end (by e.g. modifying the stack pointer in the compiled program).

The benefit of making allocations virtual until their address is observed is that you can then also optimise away some large temporary copies like in the `Box::new([0u8; VERY_LARGE_NUMBER])` case, as you wouldn't need to prove (by virtue of actually allocating) that there is actually enough free memory remaining to hold two `VERY_LARGE_NUMBER`-sized arrays.

621806614.en:
ok what about this opsem?

Any time you have a pointer, its value is always just an allocation id plus an offset.

Somewhere in the AMs global state there is a mapping from allocation id to `Option<usize>` for the actual address. The mapping for a given id can't change after initialization.

At any time during the execution of the program, the AM may stop and then do one of these two operations:
1. Crash the program (let's call this kind of crash "stack overflow")
2. Fill in an address for any allocation id currently assigned to `None`

A typed copy from a byte with provenance to a byte without provenance performs a lookup in this global state. If the value is `None`, the AM has to stop and assign an address or crash the program under a stack overflow crash. (But these may occur at any time, so this can also happen before the typed copy.)

Thanks, nice summary!
I would have written it a bit differently... I view "ghost_addr" as being part of the provenance. but that's equivalent. (Also why does it have to be a "rational"? it can just be a mathematical integer I think.) Also instead of allocation planes I just imagine all allocations having unique IDs (which they already have anyway), no need to group them in planes. Though with some of the custom allocator stuff we are planning where allocations can be created "inside" existing allocations, we'd have to represent allocations being in the same "group" or so, and then we may as well call that a "plane"... so I am warming up to the "plane" terminology. I would call it `ghost_plane` though, not `ghost_addr`, as `ghost-addr` sounds like it has the full address, not just the plane.

@_**niluxv|401145** [said](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/136281-t-opsem/topic/Do.20we.20already.20have.20overlapping.20allocations.3F.20.28OOM.20Edition.29/near/621896684):
```quote
Well, let me describe the proposal as I understand it...
```

So, I think this is still too abstract to me (is `self.ghost_cap.expose()` supposed to modify `self.ghost_addr`? And a bunch of other questions like this), but the properties seem good.

Basically, the situation is that under this model `a.addr() == b.addr()` breaks when `a` and `b` are from different allocations (have different `ghost_cap`s)?

And presumably `with_exposed_provenance(a.addr()) == with_exposed_provenance(b.addr())` doesn't save you (but while it might not work, but it also isn't UB, which, well, it better not be since it's safe). However, IIUC actually exposing the provenance would (IIUC) *does* save you? (In that it gives you something you can compare?)

The main downsides here that I see are:

1. Compatibility, since existing code may assume that addr behaves the way we've, erm, been saying it does (I could believe that this doesn't actually matter because in practice the cases where that assumption breaks in a visible way are so rare as to never happen[^1]... but I also could be wrong about this).

2. Teachability, since it seems meaningfully harder to explain than what we have currently. I think it also doesn't fit as nicely into a 'tower of weakenings' approach (which works best when the complex stuff is more permissive rather than less). This could perhaps be fixed by rethinking the tower, though. I also am less concerned about this, since the alternatives all see so awful.

3. Detectability, since there's no way to detect that `usize_a == usize_b` are integers that came from an `addr()` call, so we can't warn about this (and could only lint on the simplest of cases). And then it forces you to use `ptr::expose_provenance()` over `ptr::addr()` more of the time (since `addr()` can't be used for comparisons reliably), with all the well-documented downsides that comes with (detectability of other issues). This seems like the worst to me, but also perhaps not that bad?

That said, as always, there's a very real chance I've misunderstood something here.

[^1]: Which seems true, otherwise the 'head in sand' strategy would be far less attractive.

[^2]: Cantor's argument about the countability of rationals implies it can... although what the numerator and denominator are is completely mysterious to me, and if they are assigned in a way where the rational simplification matters for equality... I suppose a rational still could be required? I don't know. That sounds bizarre, so I'm assuming it's just an integer, basically.

621912209.en:
to summarize, the main pills to swallow with this approach are
- ptr comparison is not the same thing as addr comparison
- `expose_provenance` is it not `willreturn`, i.e., an optimization barrier. but we anyway discussed making it an inline asm blob to stop LLVM from miscompiling it so :shrug:  don't use it in your inner loop, use strict provenance there.
- `expose_provenance` is specified to potentially spontaneously abort the program. I am wondering how bad that is. We already say that the program can abort with a stack overflow basically any time (but as a QoI concern it generally won't), so this could be similar. OTOH it is a bit silly since unlike a stack overflow, we know this will actually *never* happen. There's nothing in the compiler that would introduce such OOM. So why have it in the spec in the first place? I don't have a good answer to this.

621933677.en:
@_**RalfJ|120791** [said](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/136281-t-opsem/topic/Do.20we.20already.20have.20overlapping.20allocations.3F.20.28OOM.20Edition.29/near/621901707):
```quote
I view "ghost_addr" as being part of the provenance.
```

Me too. But all previous conversations here on t-opsem that talk about provenance mean only `ghost_cap`.

```quote
Also why does it have to be a "rational"? it can just be a mathematical integer I think.
```

If you use rationals, the semantics has strictly more behaviours that are allowed. Since I can't think of any reason why unsafe code would prefer integer planes, and I can't oversee the ramifications of rational vs integers planes for optimisations, I opted to use rationals. We can always make them integers later.

```quote
instead of allocation planes I just imagine all allocations having unique IDs
```

~~Yes, that is equivalent (but you need to fix a bijection between AllocIds and rationals except 0, to use for order comparisons).~~ Edit: with comparisons it can actually make a difference.

```quote
but for expose_provenance I recall our discussion to be along the lines of "if it's not forced / on plane 0, then NB".
```

I think both options were discussed in the thread, OOM and NB. The end of the thread tended towards NB indeed, but since then there have been discussions pointing out complications that arise with NB, so I thought I'd opt for OOM. We can always change it to NB later, since `nb()` refines `oom()`. And if we allow a program to OOM at any point (which we probably need to, because of stack overflows), then `nb()` and `oom()` are equivalent programs since you can always avoid the NB by raising OOM.

621936966.en:
@_**Thom Chiovoloni|209168** [said](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/136281-t-opsem/topic/Do.20we.20already.20have.20overlapping.20allocations.3F.20.28OOM.20Edition.29/near/621906074):
```quote
is `self.ghost_cap.expose()` supposed to modify `self.ghost_addr`?
```

It is supposed to expose the provenance of the pointer. So"just" what `expose_provenance()` does without this proposal. No-one knows how it works.

```quote
Basically, the situation is that under this model `a.addr() == b.addr()` breaks when `a` and `b` are from different allocations (have different `ghost_cap`s)?
```

Yes. That comparison might yield `true` even though `a` and `b` point to different allocations. In particular, reading from `a` and `b` could give different answers. However, if you ever called `expose_provenance()` on both pointers, then you are fine (in the sense that if the comparison returns `true` then `a` and `b` actually point to the same allocation; they might still have different provenance of course).

```quote
And presumably `with_exposed_provenance(a.addr()) == with_exposed_provenance(b.addr())` doesn't save you
```

Indeed it doesn't. This is probably just equivalent to `a.addr() == b.addr()`.

```quote
The main downsides here that I see are:
```
* Compatibility.
I know. We should have done this before stabilizing `addr()`. But if "head in the sand" works, then clearly you won't run into trouble due to comparing addresses where you actually wanted pointer comparison.
* Teachability. I think this proposal is quite natural from the strict-provenance point of view.
* Detectability. I would think that many "violations" actually have `a.addr() == b.addr()` as syntactic shape.

(Btw, I don't know what your second footnote refers to. But rationals for me is just rational numbers, not some kind of syntactic fractions or something. 2/4, 1/2 and 0.5 are all the same number.)

@_**RalfJ|120791** [said](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/136281-t-opsem/topic/Do.20we.20already.20have.20overlapping.20allocations.3F.20.28OOM.20Edition.29/near/621911183):
````quote
@_**Thom Chiovoloni|209168** [said](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/136281-t-opsem/topic/Do.20we.20already.20have.20overlapping.20allocations.3F.20.28OOM.20Edition.29/near/621906074):
```quote
* And then it forces you to use `ptr::expose_provenance()` over `ptr::addr()` more of the time (since `addr()` can't be used for comparisons reliably),
```

it encourages you to compare the pointers directly rather than converting them into addresses first.
having to use expose_provenance seems pretty rare?
````

Sure, I meant for the cases where you could previously use just addr. The fact that usually you can just compare pointers is why I think it's not so bad.

> We already say that the program can abort with a stack overflow basically any time (but as a QoI concern it generally won't), so this could be similar. OTOH it is a bit silly since unlike a stack overflow, we know this will actually *never* happen

Ah, I had interpreted that as being a legit OOM case where because of the expose, we could no longer remove an allocation (and now something else will OOM, so I guess the fact that the OOM isn't in the right place for that should have tipped me off...).

> I would think that many "violations" actually have `a.addr() == b.addr()` as syntactic shape

I don't think so. I can't imagine when you would ever compare `a.addr()` to `b.addr()` directly. Maybe some arithmetic to avoid going through `ptr::wrapping_{add,sub,offset}` (because those are sometimes seen as less 'correct' for somewhat dubious reasons) or something?

One case I can imagine is `(a.addr() & SOME_MASK) == (b.addr() & SOME_MASK)`. And whether or not that's okay depends on which bits `SOME_MASK` is removing...

...

In the interest of being a bit less abstract, I looked around std a bit for things that either violate this rule or seem dubious under it. Here are some cases where addresses are compared (to things other than constants)

- https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/f207aa3913114c3326bc0b88acbd12b10244edf8/library/std/src/sys/pal/unix/stack_overflow/thread_info.rs (`errno_location().addr()` used as a thread id in a lock)

- https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/f207aa3913114c3326bc0b88acbd12b10244edf8/library/std/src/backtrace.rs#L325 (instruction pointer compared to a symbol addr. perhaps these are fine because they're code addresses, not addresses of allocations?)

- https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/f207aa3913114c3326bc0b88acbd12b10244edf8/library/std/src/sys/pal/windows/mod.rs#L72. This is subtraction and not comparison, although the result of the subtraction does get compared, so it seems similar. My assumption is that this is fine because they're from the same allocation? Or is that only the case for the other model.

- https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/f207aa3913114c3326bc0b88acbd12b10244edf8/library/std/src/sys/pal/unix/stack_overflow.rs#L110 This actually compares the faulting address to another address range. It feels like this perhaps could be a case that needs to be expose_addr? Certainly the provenances of the guardpage and the fault address are going to be wildly different... Hmmm... Or perhaps we can just declare that this is a case that is Sufficiently Magic to not be a problem?

- https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/f207aa3913114c3326bc0b88acbd12b10244edf8/library/std/src/path.rs#L1666-L1669 (more addr() on pointers from same alloc -> arith -> do stuff with result. there's a lot of this, so I'll omit the rest).

- https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/f207aa3913114c3326bc0b88acbd12b10244edf8/library/std/src/sync/mpmc/waker.rs#L71-L92 These thread ids are `addr()`s of thread locals, and are absolutely being compared. I guess they need to expose instead? Or stay as pointers (harder sell maybe)

- https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/f207aa3913114c3326bc0b88acbd12b10244edf8/library/std/src/thread/tests.rs#L149-L165 A test where the addr of a local is compared. Obviously if the code under test is correct then this is fine (same address), but otherwise ???

- There's... also a few places in std::sync that *seem* fine, but I would probably want to do a real look if this model were accepted. And also the xous sync primitives look like they probably violate it, but I don't care enough to dig into a tier3 platform I've only heard of once. (No offense meant to anybody who cares about it, I suppose.)

Anyway, perhaps figuring out if the usage is "okay" or not will get easier over time, but as it stands just from that cursory review, I would say that this makes reviewing code with `addr()` harder (and the "easiest" fix for that in a lot of cases is just to expose instead, since it doesn't require rewriting the code or carefully maintaining provenance of a pointer).

```quote
@**niluxv** As far as I can tell, LLVM never removes allocations if you compare their addresses like this
```

If you do anything interesting (including infinite loops) conditional on comparison on pointers (except equality), LLVM stops optimizing away the allocation.

However, even unobservable things like sorting a sequence of pointers, or sufficiently complex `assert_unchecked` on comparison results, tends to not get optimized away. 
idk if it's a good idea to rely on LLVM being overly careful atm.

622027700.en:
So as far as I can tell, it's *almost* the case that LLVM only removes an allocation if it can prove that the program's behavior is the same no matter which (legal) address it chooses. So the program can convert the pointer to an address and check its lower bits, which are zero in any program due to alignment. It can do math where the base address cancels out (i.e. `x - x` simplifies to `0`). Also, LLVM will optimize `ptr1.addr() == ptr2.addr()` to just `ptr1 == ptr2`.

Now the only case where this doesn't apply is that LLVM is happy to constant fold `ptr1 == ptr2` to `false` even if both pointers are removed. This is a bit unfortunate for that model because it means that it removed the allocation even though not *all* choices for `ptr1.addr()` and `ptr2.addr()` lead to the same program behavior, because the choice where both are equal has different behavior.

So because of that, we cannot just inspect all possible choices for the address and require that the program behavior must be the same no matter what the chosen address is.
